content:

Over a 600 edits have already been made under this name. None of them seem to be reflected on the nForum.

There is a strong correlation between pages edited by “p” and pages edited by “Anonymouse”, most of the articles edited by “p” have been edited by “Anonymouse” previously.

Previous discussions: https://nforum.ncatlab.org/discussion/19316/writing-in-the-nlab/ and https://nforum.ncatlab.org/discussion/19138/infinity1coproduct/.
subject: Anonymouse

content:
#2

Over a 600 edits have already been made under this name. None of them seem to be reflected on the nForum.

That user, whoever it may be, has clearly not read the nLab’s HomePage which says

For all but the most trivial edits (correcting spelling or punctuation, etc), we ask that you announce your changes at the nForum using the box at the bottom of the edit page.

A lot of the problems historically with users editing the nLab comes from them not writing a comment explaining what exactly has changed on the article, meaning that nobody on the nForum notices anything. Especially if there are any errors with what’s being added to the page, those errors can sit there for years before somebody notices. It’s going to be a bigger problem in the future when people try to post LLM output on the nLab, since LLMs are known to hallucinate.

Maybe it’s time for the nLab to enforce writing a comment for any substantial edit made by users, similar to any new articles created by users, so that they do appear on the nForum. Perhaps some limit of if you added, removed, and/or changed more than X characters to an article, then you need to write a comment before you can submit your edit, with X being some number defined to exclude trivial edits.
subject: Anonymouse

content:

#5 Thanks for the heads up.

We can ask the technical team to block the account “p”.

But if that user could actually be identified personally and talked to and brought to reason, that would be a better solution. Madeleine may know them?

I suggest: If anyone can, let’s make an attempt to contact the user and if that fails let’s block them again.

P.S. More software security measures might indeed help. Trouble is we are lacking volunteers to work on the software. Eventually the time may come that we need a login mechanism for nLab edits. With that not available, for the time being we need to rely on social dynamics.

#9

What’s the point of the technical team then?

The technical team is ensuring the operation of our server.

(Many thanks to Christian, Felix, and Hannes for their work on this! Without them we would be toast.)

They are not developing our software. Consensus is that the nLab software is undevelopable and would need a complete rewrite from scratch. We have been trying to hire a software engineer, but it didn’t work out.

Ah I see, Christian Sattler updated the readme an year ago to say that the nLab software is in maintenance mode and no longer being actively developed:

https://github.com/ncatlab/nlab/commit/b7723854344e28b7986badb35981c70a3f0c954e

Previously there seems to have been a person called Richard Williamson who was involved in the development of the nLab.
subject: Anonymouse

content:
#11 Previously we had a sequence of volunteers who worked on the software. First Andrew Stacey, then Adeel Khan, I think, later Richard Williamson. We haven’t had such a volunteer since.

The technical team has emphasized that the various edits made by the previous admins (maybe particularly towards the end) have brought the code base into a state that is practically unmaintainable now.

It always struck me that in a community rich in computer scientist we would end up in such a situation, but that’s what we have.
subject: Anonymouse

content: #12 What were the obstacles to finding a new developer?
subject: Anonymouse

content:
#13 Payment. A candidate that we finally found expected a salary competitive with that of a full-time job in the software industry.

(At some point a couple of years back we had sizeable funds available for the nLab at CQTS, but not that sizeable. I apologize to those involved in the process if it was me who miscommunicated this point. It remains hard for non-IT people to appreciate the resources necessary to fix what looks like a fairly primitive text-display software.)
